summary: Describes five kinds of SNMP applications that use an SNMP engine: command generators, command responders, notification originators, notification receivers and proxy forwarders. It also defines MIB modules for specifying targets of management operations, filtering notifications and configuring proxy forwarding.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3413 describes five jobs that SNMP applications can perform: make management requests, answer them, send alerts, receive alerts, and forward messages. It also defines MIB modules for configuring message destinations, notification filters, and forwarding rules.

subtitle: The five kinds of SNMP application and the MIB modules that configure targets, notifications, and proxies.

tldr.problem: An SNMP engine needs applications that generate requests, answer requests, send and receive notifications, and forward messages. These applications also need configurable targets and rules.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3413 defines five application types, procedures for sending and processing SNMP messages, and three MIB modules for targets, notifications, and proxy forwarding.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3413 is Internet Standard STD 62 and obsoletes RFC 2573. The batch metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Five Kinds of SNMP Application
sections.content:
A command generator starts Read-Class or Write-Class requests and processes responses. A command responder receives those requests, performs the operation under access control, and sends a response. A notification originator monitors for events and creates notification messages; a notification receiver listens for those messages and answers confirmed notifications.

A proxy forwarder passes SNMP messages to other engines. One SNMP engine can have more than one application type, and implementing a proxy forwarder is optional.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP applications can ask questions, answer them, send alerts, receive alerts, or pass messages onward. One SNMP engine may perform more than one of these jobs.

sections.title: Management Targets
sections.content:
A management target describes where and how an application sends a message. It combines destination information, consisting of a transport domain and transport address, with SNMP parameters such as the message-processing model, security model, security level, and security name.

The SNMP-TARGET-MIB keeps destination addresses in one table and SNMP parameters in another. These tables can have a many-to-many relationship: several destinations can use one parameter set, or one destination can use several parameter sets. Tags can group destination entries for selection.
sections.plainLanguage: A target entry combines a destination address with instructions for the SNMP message. Tables let several destinations share settings, and tags let an application select a group of destinations.

sections.title: Generating and Answering Requests
sections.content:
A command generator sends a PDU through the SNMP Dispatcher with the destination, context, protocol, and security settings. If it expects a response, it stores the returned sendPduHandle so it can match the response to the request. A response with mismatched message, security, context, PDU version, or request-id values is discarded.

A command responder registers the request types it handles before processing messages. For each requested object, it checks access against the relevant MIB view. Access failures can produce an authorizationError or genError response; an unknown or unavailable context instead increments its corresponding counter and produces a report. A responder should call returnResponsePdu even after an error.
sections.plainLanguage: The application that asks a question keeps a handle to match the reply. The application that answers checks access to each requested object before returning information.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Notifications
sections.content:
A notification originator determines the context, destinations, PDU type, and any retry behavior. It applies configured filters and access checks before sending to each target. For a confirmed notification, it caches target information and retries if an acknowledgement does not arrive within the applicable interval, up to the configured retry count.

A notification receiver registers the notification types it wants. For an unconfirmed PDU, later handling depends on the implementation. For a confirmed PDU, it returns a response using the received request-id and variable bindings, with error-status and error-index set to zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender chooses which approved targets receive each notification. A confirmed notification expects an acknowledgement; the receiver returns one with the same request identifier.

sections.title: How a Proxy Forwarder Works
sections.content:
In this RFC, a proxy forwarder routes messages according to context, without examining which managed object types the messages contain. This differs from a command responder, which processes a request based on the managed objects it names. Proxy forwarding is optional.

For a request, the proxy translates the incoming target into one outgoing target, sends the request, and caches information needed to match the response. It restores the original request-id when returning the response. For notifications, it can translate to multiple targets and forwards the message's variable bindings without applying notification filtering or access control to those bindings.
sections.plainLanguage: A proxy forwarder chooses where a message goes based on its context, not on the objects named inside it. It sends replies back to the original requester and can pass notifications to several destinations.

sections.title: The Three Configuration MIBs
sections.content:
The SNMP-TARGET-MIB defines destinations and the message parameters used with them. The SNMP-NOTIFICATION-MIB selects target addresses for notifications, chooses trap or inform behavior, and defines notification filters. A target can be selected by a tag on its address-table entry.

The SNMP-PROXY-MIB defines translations used to forward messages. For a request, a matching row selects one outgoing target; for notifications, matching rows can select multiple targets. Together, these modules let an SNMP entity expose target, notification, and proxy configuration through MIB objects.
sections.plainLanguage: One MIB lists destinations and message settings, another selects and filters notifications, and a third defines forwarding rules. Administrators can use these tables to configure where each kind of message goes.

sections.title: Access Control and Sensitive Configuration
sections.content:
SNMP applications may have direct access to MIB instrumentation, so the RFC says they must apply access control strictly. A notification generator must not reveal information that access control would normally hide, even if it obtains that information through another source.

The MIB modules can hold sensitive configuration information. The RFC says a security administrator may wish to limit access to them.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications must respect the same access rules as other SNMP operations. Limit access to configuration tables when they contain sensitive information.
